utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-04-75-T, The Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. May we have the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. For the Prosecution, Douglas Stringer; Lisa Biersay; case manager, Thomas Laugel; and legal intern, Moritz von Normann.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic and Christopher Gosnell, with legal intern, Sunna Aevarsdottir. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stringer, I heard you had some preliminaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. There was just one housekeeping matter from yesterday. At page 11.105 of yesterday's transcript, the Chamber gave an MFI number to a document pending translation related to a footnote. The document was 65 ter 1939.13 and the MFI number given was 3252. We're informing the Chamber that the translation has been obtained and the revised translation has now been uploaded into e-court and so we're tendering that exhibit into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked. Mr. Zivanovic, is your next witness ready?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I hope so, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Can we bring the witness in. Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I rise because there is an additional party present in the courtroom. I believe it's Mr. Terzic. So perhaps his appearance should be also on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I wanted to do that while addressing Mr. Seselj, but that's also a good suggestion, Ms. Biersay. So if we can have your appearance for the record, Mr. Terzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So Mr. Milan Terzic, the legal advisor for --

utterances.speaker: MR. TERZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Seselj. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Could you state your name and date of birth for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am Dr. Vojislav Seselj. I was born on the 11th of October, 1954.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Seselj, you are about to read the solemn declaration by which witnesses commit themselves to tell the truth. I need to point out that the solemn declaration that you are about to make does expose you to the penalties for perjury should you give misleading or untruthful testimony to this Tribunal. Could I ask you to read the solemn declaration now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, before you commence your evidence, although I believe that you must be well aware of this, I must draw your attention to Rule 90(E) of the Tribunal's Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Under these rules you may object to answer any question from the Defence, the Prosecutor, or even from the Judges if you believe that your answer might incriminate you. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that might amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you and, as a consequence, you refuse to answer the question, the Tribunal nevertheless has the power to compel you to answer the question, but in that situation the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony, compelled in such circumstances, would not be used in the case against you or in any case that might be laid against you for any offence, save and except the offence of giving false testimony. To help you to assess weather a question or the answer to a question could have the potential of self-incrimination, the Court granted you at your request to be assisted in Court by your legal advisor, Mr. Milan Terzic, whom I welcome in the courtroom. Mr. Zivanovic, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, although we've met already, I will introduce myself for the record. My name is Zoran Zivanovic. I am the Defence counsel of Goran Hadzic in these proceedings. First of all, let me ask you which schools have you completed?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: Primary school, high school, the faculty of law, post-graduate studies, earning first the degree of master and then doctor, Ph.D.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you tell us where have you been employed in your life?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: First of all, I worked at the faculty of law at the University of Sarajevo. I was assistant professor in the Department of International Relations, but after being expelled from the League of Communists and pronounced unfit to work with students, I was removed from the chair and I was moved to the Institute for Social Studies in a status equal to assistant professor. In 1991, I was elected lecturer at the law faculty in Pristina and in 1999, I became full-time professor at the law school of the University of Belgrade, when the mafia regime of Zoran Djindjic expelled me from that position on the 5th of October, 2000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, just one moment. Mr. Seselj, could I ask you to observe a pause between the question and your answer. That's the time the interpreters need to finish the interpretation of the question. Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I have noticed a mistake in the transcript. At the beginning, you said you were at the faculty of law in Sarajevo as assistant professor.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: No, it was the faculty of political science. I graduated from the faculty of law in Sarajevo. First I was assistant on a trial period and then I was assistant professor at the faculty of political science.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you kindly describe your political career.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: After being expelled from the then-only ruling party, which was in 1971, I gradually grew into an anti-Communist dissident and that process lasted until 1984, when I was arrested. And because of an unpublished paper, a study called "What To Do," I was convicted to eight years imprisonment. The supreme court reduced that sentence to four years, and the federal court reduced it to one year and four months, which I served. First of all, I was convicted for jeopardizing the socio-political order, and later, the conviction was requalified into a conviction for hostile propaganda.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you just repeat once again, how did the federal court reduce the initial sentence meted out by the appellate court?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: In 1976, the federal court reduced my sentence to one year and four months, which I served.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction: One year and ten months.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said you became an anti-Communist dissident. Could you describe the circumstances under which it happened. What was the situation in the country that led you to those convictions?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: It was still the regime of an open Tito's -- Titoist dictatorship. There was no freedom of thought. There was no freedom of press. There was no parliamentary/political system. It was impossible to establish political parties. And there was not even free association of citizens. Everybody who opposed that regime, who was idealogically in a different position, anybody who was opposed to that system, to that regime, was persecuted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us briefly before you came to this Tribunal, were you ever convicted; and, if so, why?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: I was convicted several times but never for dishonourable criminal acts. When I say that, I mean I was convicted exclusively for political reasons, the first time in Sarajevo over an unpublished text that the secret police seized from me on a train; later, during the Milosevic regime in Serbia, I was convicted another four times before Milosevic came to power. In 1984, I was arrested along with a group of people who attended a lecture of Milan Djilas at the illegal law school of the university in Belgrade. The police arrested us, kept us for a few days, and then released us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please speak a little more slowly so it can all be correctly recorded and interpreted.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: I have been trying already. Milosevic's regime arrested me and convicted me another four or five times. The first two times -- in fact, the first time, it was in September 1990 for organising the signing of a petition to remove the mausoleum of Josip Broz Tito from Belgrade and for signing up volunteers for departure to Knin where they would defend the Serbian Krajina. Then I was convicted to 15 days in prison. Then over some protests dispersed by the police, I was convicted to another 25 days imprisonment and I served those two sentences together. My party was outlawed. I can't say it was illegal, but the regime had refused to register it. So a group of citizens, my closest assistants, nominated me for president of the republic, so the regime released me early. And there were some minor offences, misdemeanours, where I was tried by misdemeanour courts which belonged to the executive branch of government. In 1984 [as interpreted], I was arrested over an incident in the federal parliament for which I was not responsible. It was the speaker of the parliament who was responsible, but based on false testimony, I was again convicted by a misdemeanour court to one month's imprisonment. I was a federal MP, and you know in the civilised world the executive branch of government does not have the right to judge members of the legislative branch. So an executive court cannot try a member of parliament; only regular courts could do that. However, this rule was violated at that time. After that, while I was still serving my prison sentence, one suspended sentence was reversed into one month's imprisonment again over an incident in the federal parliament when the security detail of the parliament tried forcibly to remove a member of the Serbian Radical Party and we, the other members, opposed them. Since I was the leader of that group, they convicted only me. I served those sentences together, four months in total. And the last time I was arrested in the beginning of June 1994 where the police in Gnjline prohibited a rally of the Serbian Radical Party without any legal basis. And then they staged an incident. One policemen dressed in mufti provoked an incident and then the police arrested all those present. Again, I was convicted over a misdemeanour to two months in prison, and I served that sentence in Gnjline which is in Serbian Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, just a moment, please. At page 7, line 2, there is mention of a year at the beginning of line 12. In the following sentence: "And there were some minor offences, misdemeanours, where I was tried by misdemeanour courts which belonged to the executive branch of government. In" -- and there is the year: "I was arrested over an incident in the federal parliament ..." Mr. Seselj, what was the year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That's what I thought I heard. On the record it is 1984, so the record has to be corrected. Please continue, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1984 is the year when I was convicted in Sarajevo to four years in prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you tell us, proceedings are ongoing before this Tribunal against you. On what charges?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: Before this Tribunal, I'm on trial on false charges. It's been going on for 12 years. They tried in umpteen ways to judge me, to convict me, but they have failed. And I am expecting very soon an acquittal and indemnity to the tune of $12 million. I was on trial for war crimes that I had nothing to do with. I was charged based on the fabrications of various false witnesses who had been coached to accuse me. However, my Defence was so successful that the Trial Chamber simply has no basis to convict me. I have been waiting for this acquittal for 12 years. I cannot be allowed to go to Belgrade because I am dangerous to the traitor authorities that are in power there, and they cannot convict me because they have no reason to. That's why they are holding me in suspense. I am now in the courtroom for the first time after two and a half years. Such things never happen anywhere in the civilised world. Here in the Hague Tribunal, I was convicted three times for the completely invented offence of contempt of court. In the civilised world, such an offence is usually punished by a fine or a disciplinary punishment. It never happened in the civilised world that an accused charged with the most serious crimes could be convicted during the trial three times for contempt of court. That could happen only at the Hague Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you also tell us how did you end up in the Detention Unit of ICTY?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: On the 24th of February, 2003, I left Belgrade to arrive to The Hague on a regular plane. I bought the ticket myself, and I planned to finish some business with the Dutch queen. When the aeroplane landed at the Amsterdam airport, the Dutch police insisted that I be the first to get off the plane. I ended expecting to be welcomed, and the police took me directly to the runway instead of taking the corridor like other passengers. I thought that perhaps there would be a welcome with the guards, but instead of that, they put me in a police car and they brought me to Scheveningen, and they are still not letting me go since that time when they brought me here. Actually, they wanted to set me free but to have me sit under house arrest in Belgrade. I've been here for 12 years in detention, and it would be another seven or eight years in Belgrade under house arrest and then they wouldn't have to make the judgement ever. They would send me away from here. I would no longer be a problem in The Hague, and at home the regime would have to keep me under house arrest, with no end in sight until I die. That was the idea, but I discerned what the idea was and I refused to leave with any limitations whatsoever being imposed on me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, the 24th of February, 2003, when you arrived here to The Hague, did you know that there was an indictment that was issued by ICTY against you?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, I learned that the indictment was there even before it was made public. I learned that on the 25th of January. One of my men who was working for the Prosecutor's office at ICTY at the time told me that. He used to supply me with information at the time. And I immediately held a press conference at which I made it public. And the indictment was unpacked only about 20 days later. And when after my press conference the journalists officially asked ICTY representatives whether it was true that there has been an indictment against me, they received answers that were imprecise and indefinite, "We don't know, there's nothing yet," and so on. So I had been informed almost 20 days before the OTP officially made this public.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Have you testified in any other case before ICTY until now?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: I testified in the case against Slobodan Milosevic for 14 days, and I testified in the proceedings against Radovan Karadzic. That was two days, if I remember properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Today you have said inter alia that you were a member of a party which was not illegal but which the regime had refused to register. Would you please tell us what was the name of that party?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: The name of that party was the Serbian Chetnik Movement, actually. Our first name in January 1990 was the Serbian Freedom Movement. Then, when Vuk Draskovic was excluded from the Serbian National Renewal, with the Draskovic-led wing, we united into a party which was called the Serbian Renewal Movement. Draskovic was then removed from his position as president, but he did not acknowledge this removal. He rallied his supporters and he acted as if they were the Serbian Renewal Movement. And that lasted for almost a month. There were two parties with the same name, and the registration of political parties had not yet begun at the time. We believed that it made no sense to focus all our energy on competing with Draskovic in order to determine which party was the original one, especially as Draskovic was supported by the regime at the time and by the regime-run media. So we decided to change the party's name into the Serbian Chetnik Movement. The then-Communist regime had much ideological prejudice against the Chetnik movement from the Second World War which used to be anti-Communist, but it was a liberation movement anyway led by Draza Mihajlovic. That was the first anti-Fascist movement in the occupied Europe. The Communists only appeared later once Hitler had attacked the Soviet Union, and it was under Stalin's instructions that they began the uprising whereas Draza Mihajlovic began the uprising spontaneously and was acknowledged by the exiled government in London. Because of the ideological prejudice the then-Communist regime refused to register the Serbian Chetnik Movement. However, we continued to be active as an unregistered party and we had quite a number of members and supporters. And then in February 1991, we united with most of the Municipal Boards of the National Radical Party to form the Serbian Radical Party. That Serbian Radical Party soon became one of the major political parties in Serbia. Unfortunately, after being attacked viciously by western intelligence services and the pro-western mafia regime led by Boris Tadic in Belgrade, there was an attempted coup within the Serbian Radical Party. Those who had attempted to lead the coup failed but then they left the party, formed a new one. They formed the Progressive Party and were then financially and politically supported by the regime, which has weakened the Serbian Radical Party to a significant degree. And today we are not a parliamentary party any longer. However, I hope that as soon as in a few days' time I'll return to Belgrade. Once I am acquitted before this Tribunal, I hope that the party will soon recover and will again be among the strongest political parties there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I think that in the transcript something has been left out. You have mentioned Draza Mihajlovic and you also mentioned London, but it was not recorded in which context you mentioned London.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: Colonel Draza Mihajlovic started an uprising against the German occupiers in Serbia in May 1941 by forming the Serbian Chetnik Movement and by launching the first attacks against the Germans. A relative of mine, Veselin Misita, was one of Draza's commanders holding the rank of lieutenant-colonel. He liberated on the 31st of August 1941 the town of Loznica. He liberated it from the Germans. That was the first major allied victory over the Germans in the entire territory of occupied Europe. Of course, the Communists at dusk on the same day killed Lieutenant-Colonel Misita from behind his back. As for Draza Mihajlovic, as soon as he started fighting the Germans, he was acknowledged, recognised by the Yugoslav exiled government seated in London at the time. They awarded him the rank of army general, appointed him as defence minister, and he was then actually one of the key commanders of the anti-Hitler coalition. But due to various Churchill's tricks and the deals he had made with Stalin, the western allies withdrew their support for Draza Mihajlovic in 1943 and began to assist the Communists openly. So Churchill's treason of Draza Mihajlovic brought us in a situation in which we had to spend 50 years under a bloody Communist dictatorship from which we haven't recovered to this day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, when I look back to the clarification question you put to Mr. Seselj and the answer he gave to that, I would like to -- "warn" is too harsh a word, but to tell you that how interesting these lessons in history and Serb history may be, as long as you know that it is on your time with this witness and you don't have a problem with it, I won't make a problem of it. But it is on your time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honour, thank you for that warning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will only ask you another thing regarding your last answer. If you can tell us as briefly as possible whether General Mihajlovic, as the leader of this movement, was ever awarded by the western allies for his contribution to the victory in the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: General Mihajlovic received the highest US medals, the Medal of Honour from the US Congress. It was only after 40 years or so that the US ambassador in Belgrade delivered this medal to General Mihajlovic's daughter. After the war, by a trick, the Communists managed to capture Draza Mihajlovic. There was a staged trial and he was shot. And to this day, it's not known where his grave is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And another question. Do you know whether, after the war, a significant number of the members of this movement, that is to say, a great number of Chetniks, found refuge in western countries?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: A number of Chetniks found refuge in France, England, the United States of America, Canada, Australia, and some other countries, but that was a smaller number. However, a greater number of Chetniks were shot by Communists at the end of the war, in the first days after the end of the war. There are mass graves of Chetniks who had been shot in Serbia, in practically every town. Even though Boris Tadic's regime was traitorist, he began digging up those mass graves. When Tomislav Nikolic and Aleksandar Vucic came to power, the digging of mass graves was immediately stopped and the process of legal rehabilitation of Draza Mihajlovic was slowed down. This is all in accordance with Tomislav Nikolic's announcement that he would continue his policy along Tito's path.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just another question with regard to this and we will move to another topic. Do you know whether any of the people from the Chetnik movement who were granted asylum in western countries were ever prosecuted for any crimes they had committed in the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: No, never. They were respected in these countries. They were honoured. They were entitled to form their own veterans' organisations, and these organisations were active up until the time when the Chetniks died out. I'm not sure whether there are any left living. In the meantime they all died.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You have said that eventually the Serbian Radical Party was formed. Have you been its president all along?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, and I continue to be the president of the Serbian Radical Party to this very day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Will you please tell us, what was the substance of the Serbian Radical Party's programme?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: The Serbian Radical Party advocated the unification. We wanted Yugoslavia to survive, of course, but when we realised that this wouldn't work when the Slovenians and the Croats had started their separatist uprising, we then advocated the formation of Greater Serbia that would include all the Serbian lands, which means today's Serbia, including Kosovo and Metohija, whose independence we shall never acknowledge. Then Macedonian, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro, Dubrovnik, Dalmatia, Lika, Banja, Kordun, Slavonia and Baranja.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And this concept of Greater Serbia, did it include the idea of ethnic cleansing, cleaning the territories from members of other ethnic or religious groups?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: Absolutely not. We did not come out with a new idea of Greater Serbia. That idea has existed for several hundred years in the Serbian people. The first who had this project to unify all Serbian lands was the last Serbian despot that was Count Djordje Brankovic. At the time of the siege of Vienna, when the Turks were defeated in Vienna, Count Djordje Brankovic addressed the Austro-Hungarian tsar with the proposal that all the Serbian lands be liberated from the Turks, that a Serbian despot be established, and that in a way it would be a part of the Austrian empire. The Austrian emperor agreed. He confirmed the title of despot for Djordje Brankovic. He also awarded him the title of Austrian count, which was an aristocratic title, and helped the realisation of this plan. Everything was successful initially. The Austrian army, greatly helped by the Serbs who had started the uprising, and with the help of the Serbs who were living within the Austrian borders at the time, this army reached as far as Skopje. Famous General Pikolomini was leading the Austrian army in Skopje. He fell ill. He contracted the plague. He was taken to Prizren, to the military hospital, where he died. The new commander of the Austrian army was unable to battle the Turks any longer, and the Austrians had to withdraw all the way to the Danube. And then if you're interested about Greater Serbia, I wanted to tell you how old this project was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. You need to slow down because your words cannot be recorded faithfully if you speak fast. You have already told us how old the project is. I'm interested in something else. The idea of the Greater Serbia, was it advocated by another political party in Serbia in the 1990s of last century?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: Absolutely not. Only the Serbian Radical Party advocated that project. The project encompassed the territories that I have already mentioned. All of our documents from the Serbian Freedom Movement to the Serbian Radical Party, we directly and clearly advocate the unity and brotherhood of the Serbs of Orthodox faith, the Serbs of the Catholic faith, and the Serbs of Muslim faith, as well as the Serbs of the Protestant faith. And you know, in the entire territory that I have mentioned, only Serbian language is spoken. For decades the Croats have tried to corrupt the language but inventing new words, but they can't change it completely. Bosnian Muslims also speak Serbian. I know that the Hague Tribunal created a very vile term, "B/C/S," but this is Serbian. The global linguistics recognises the language as exclusively Serb language. There were Croats, however. There was a Croatian nation and the language in question is Cakavian. However, in 1850, Croatian intellectuals, in agreement with Vuk Karadzic and Djuro Danicic, decided that Serbian would also become their official language. That was the foundation for all the Serb Catholics to become part of the Croatian body. And the war in the Balkans was the war amongst the Serbs themselves, the Serbs of Orthodox faith, the Serbs of Catholic faith, and Serbs of Muslim faith. We are all one and the same people. We are all Serbs, but the western powers sow the seeds of evil amongst us. We bled. We lost a lot of life in order to support America and western Europe, who are our traditional enemies. That was all to their own good.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you now tell us in the 1990s of last century, what was the position of the Socialist Party of Serbia, the SPS?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: The Socialist Party of Serbia literally inherited power from the League of Communists. Overnight, they just changed their name. They pretended that the League of Communists had united with the Socialist Alliance of Working People and became the Socialist Party. Only the name was changed. Everything else remained the same. Milosevic was still the leader of the party. They still held power in their hands. And in December, they ran in the presidential and parliamentary elections and they were victorious. There were also local elections and they were victorious almost everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In December of what year?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: 1990. The Serbian Radical Party was not allowed to run in those elections. I was a presidential candidate on behalf of a group of citizens. I did not record significant results, but I became very popular through my television appearances because that was the only time ever that I could ever appear on TV during the pre-election campaign. Before that, television could only smear my name, and I was not allowed to say anything on TV.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What was the relationship between the Serbian Radical Party on the one hand and the Socialist Party of Serbia on the other hand?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: We were extremely opposed to each other. We were in constant conflict with Milosevic's regime. When you look at some other opposition parties, save for Vuk Draskovic, Milosevic absolutely didn't arrest anybody. Draskovic was arrested on two occasions when he caused bloodshed and death on the streets of Belgrade. There was never any blood at our rallies. But I was always targeted by that regime as its most serious enemy and opponent.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that inter alia on one occasion you were arrested because you were in charge of an action to register volunteers who were going to be sent to Croatia, i.e., Krajina.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Then I didn't understand you.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: We didn't -- didn't want to send volunteers to Croatia ever. Although that was part of my propaganda, I used to say, "I'm going to send Chetniks to capture Tudjman," and so on and so forth. But as a matter of fact, we never sent anybody to Croatia. We sent our volunteers exclusively to the territory of Serbian Krajina to defend the Serbian people and not to attack the Croatian people. They just went to defend what was Serbian. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, at that time when you rallied volunteers, the state system of Yugoslavia was still functioning. There were institutions that were responsible for defending all citizens irrespective of their religion and faith. Can you please tell us why you did what you did, in view of the fact that there were the police, the military and other institutions who were in charge of that?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: When Tudjman took over in Croatia and immediately expelled or removed the Serbian people from the constitution, although the Serbian people was a constituent people in Croatia and equal to the Croatian people but Tudjman wanted to transform them into a national minority, a lot of confrontations started happening. The Croats started prosecuting Serbs. Already in 1990, Serb refugees started arriving in Serbia. There were clashes in the field because Croats wanted to disarm forcibly the Serb police stations. Many Serbs were arrested, beaten, and many were killed as well. The Yugoslav People's Army which was duty-bound to protect the territorial integrity, sovereignty and integrity, of the state as prescribed by the constitution, was not able to do that. At first the JNA was neutral and passive. And the Serbs in Serbian Krajina were simply helpless. And then we started volunteers from Serbia illegally, starting with April 1991 until the end of August 1991. It was only sometime at the beginning of September 1991, when the JNA got involved in armed activities, we made an agreement with the General Staff of the JNA to send our volunteers into JNA units. Before the 1st of September, we did have paramilitary formations; we did have our own armed forces that fought to defend the Serbian villages in Eastern Slavonia and Western Srem. Our volunteers won a huge victory in Borovo Selo on the 2nd of May, 1991, fighting against the Croatian special police, for example. We did send those volunteers but we hid the fact from the regime in Belgrade. The JNA and the Serb police tried to prevent us from doing that. The Hague OTP has a large number of documents which show how the police reacted to our attempts. However, since the volunteers were very good warriors and since the JNA finally realised that they were between the rock and the hard place and that they had to come to the Ustasha regime in Croatia since the Croats had already blockaded the JNA barracks in many places and jeopardized the lives of officers and their families, when a direct clash was already present between the Croatian paramilitaries and the JNA, we reached an agreement with the JNA that there would be no paramilitary formations but, rather, that our volunteers would be sent under the command of the JNA. In other words, before the 1st of September, I was the number one man, the commander, as it were, but obviously I was not the effective commander in the field but I was the leader of those paramilitary formations. After that, we sent all of them to JNA units, and after that, we never had any paramilitary unit. Not in Serbian Krajina, not in Republika Srpska. Nowhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us when did you first meet Milan Babic?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: I first met Milan Babic in 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And when did you meet Milan Martic?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: At the same time as Milan Babic. Milan Babic was the president of Knin municipality. He was also the president of the association of municipalities of Southern Dalmatia and Lika, if my memory served me right, but it's neither here nor there, whereas Milan Martic was the chief of the police station in Knin. That was before the setting up of Serbian Krajina which was later to become the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know when the Serbian Democratic Party was set up?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: It was established sometime in the beginning of 1990 or perhaps before that. I'm not sure. However, a majority of the Serbian population in the then-Federal Republic of Croatia did not vote for the Serbian Democratic Party. They voted for a Croat, Ivica Racan, and his Party of Democratic Changes. That's what it was known as. It was the former League of Communists. They thought that if Racan won, Croatia would remain part of Yugoslavia. The Serb people would remain equal. They were against Tudjman, but they did not want to support the Serbian National Party. It was only when they realised that everything was staged in Croatia, that the Roman Catholic church got involved as well as Ivica Racan and many other factors, all with a view to securing Tudjman's victory, and when they realised what Tudjman's regime was all about, the Serbian people turned towards the Serbian Democratic Party and that's when its establishment started in all Serbian lands, in all the territories inhabited by the Serbs. For example, the mayor of Vukovar, Slavko Dokmanovic, was elected in 1990 as Racan's party candidate, not as a candidate of the Serbian Democratic Party, because he also thought that that party guaranteed the state unity and equality. But it was a deception, it was all a big lie.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know when the Serbian National Council was established?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: The Serbian National Council of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I mean the Serbian National Council of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell you that, not with precision. I know when the Serbian National Council of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem was established. If you will believe me, I don't even know that the Serbian National Council of Serbian Krajina ever existed. The head of the Serbian National Council of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem was Koncarevic and the other one was Petkovic. One of them was the president of the assembly and the other one was the president of the executive board. And that could have been sometime in mid 1991 or perhaps in the first half of 1991. I knew both very well, Ilija Koncarevic and Ilija Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember your first visit to Eastern Slavonia? When was that?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: That was on 9 March 1991. I remember the date because on that same day, Vuk Draskovic, leading pro-western political parties, created chaos and caused bloodshed in Belgrade. I visited Eastern Slavonia and Western Srem. I toured seven villages and I held political rallies in all of them - Trpinje, Bobota, Borovo Selo, Mirkovci, perhaps Tenja, Negoslavci. I can't remember -- Sodolovci as well. I really can't remember all of their names because later on I went to many other villages. So I really can't be sure of that particular visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whom you met in 1991? I'm speaking about the political leaders of Eastern Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: I met Ilija Koncarevic, Ilija Petkovic, somewhat later Suskocanin who was the commander of the Territorial Defence of Borovo Selo. You know, I met a lot of people. I really can't remember all of them. I'm a politician. I meet thousands of people, and if I don't meet certain people several times on special occasions, I lose sight of them and I forget them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned during your testimony that your volunteers were in Borovo Selo. Could you please tell us why? Who was it who wanted their presence there?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: Sometime in April or in the first half of April 1991, I visited Borovo Selo and I met Vukasin Suskocanin there. He was the commander of the Territorial Defence of that village. He asked me to send volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party. I appointed one of my escorts - one was already there, Mladen Todosijevic and Oliver Denis Baret, who was there of his own will - to be the commander and the deputy commander of those volunteers, to put in place conditions for their accommodation. And as soon as I returned to Belgrade, we sent a large group of volunteers there. There were a lot of tensions there between Tudjman's regime and the Serbian villagers. There were barricades on the roads. There was shooting. And sometime before the 2nd of May an agreement was reached between the local Serbs and Croats to reduce tensions, to normalise the situation, to remove the barricades, and to create a peaceful atmosphere which would be conducive to political negotiations. The Serbs believed that. Barricades were removed. Lots of the volunteers returned to Serbia and only 16 or 17 of them remained. One or two were from the Serbian Renewal Movement and the rest were from the Serbian Radical Party. Knowing full well that the Serbs relaxed, that they went back to their field-work because it was the beginning of May, the sowing season and all the sowing was done manually, the Serbs were mainly in their fields. We're talking about a rural area. The volunteers returned to Serbia. Only a small group remained. The Croats organised themselves. They got on a bus and onto cars. And on the 2nd of May, sometime around noon, they stormed into Borovo Selo and started shooting from automatic weapons. On that occasion, they killed an unarmed person, Vojislav Milic, who was a volunteer of the Serbian Renewal Movement from Valjevo. He was sitting in front of the cultural hall. He was reading his newspaper. He didn't have any weapons. The Croats opened fire and killed him there and then. The rest of the volunteers were taken by surprise; however, they grabbed their weapons and they returned fire. Croats were panic-stricken. As a result there was a lot of casualties. They admitted that 12 of their policemen were killed; according to our information, many more were killed. They never counted among the victims the bodies of the policemen who lay strewn in the cornfields and the foreign mercenaries. There were already Kurds as members of their paramilitary formations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just one more question regarding these visits of yours. Do you remember when you visited Baranja?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: I visited Baranja for the first time also in April 1991, a couple of days after visiting Borovo Selo. I returned to Belgrade from Borovo Selo, spent a few days there and then went to Baranja. I can't remember the exact date but the OTP has all this information. They have the entire text of the speech I held in Jagodnjak near Beli Manastir. Because of that speech, the Croatian regime, led by Tudjman, convicted me to four years in prison in absentia, and when an amnesty was proclaimed, I was amnestied as well. Four and a half years was that sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was there an a particular place, in those early days before that agreement you reached with the JNA, where the volunteers were trained?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes. In Prigrevica, near the Danube riverbank at an abandoned farm, we got hold of some facilities where the volunteers were put up. We set up a training camp led by Jovo Ostojic. Later on I proclaimed him a Chetnik Vojvoda, duke. We sent up that centre together with the association of Serbs from Croatia. Those were Serbs from various parts of the then-Federal Republic -- federative part of Yugoslavia that Croatia was, and they were mainly officers led by General Dusan Pekic. Sometime in summer 1991, we agreed that volunteers from individual political parties would not go separately to the front line. Instead, we agreed that we should unite jointly, send the volunteers who would have the same insignia. We introduced the insignia with a Serbian flag then because we knew we had to remove the five-pointed star which was the insignia before, because they would not fight under the emblems of Yugoslavia. Some political parties accepted but didn't do anything. Some refused but we, the Radical Party, started to send volunteers intensively in that way, and initially illegally we trained them in Prigrevica. During the first months, the police failed to detect it. Our volunteers crossed the Danube illegally in civilian clothes and then, on the other side, they would receive uniforms or parts of uniforms, but they earned a very good reputation as fighters on the front line. The Serbian people held them in high esteem and respected them. The Yugoslav People's Army realised that, and when they had no choice any longer, they addressed the Serbian Radical Party and in August 1991, many high-ranking officers of the JNA from the General Staff passed through my office and we agreed about everything. And from the 1st of September that year, we started sending our volunteers exclusively through the JNA. We even decided to return the volunteers who had already been sent back to Serbia, and the order was given that the volunteers should return to Serbia and then redeployed through the JNA. We observed this agreement strictly and we no longer from that point on had any unit that could be called paramilitary. They were under the command of the state army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could we just clarify because the record doesn't reflect everything precisely. You mentioned the name of a person who was then, I believe, the commander of your staff, or Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: The Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you repeat the name. What did he ask from the volunteers who were already on the ground?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: It was Ljubisa Petkovic. And he demanded in a letter that the OTP has that all volunteers immediately return to Belgrade. There may have been even been a deadline for their return. There were some volunteers who refused to go back, for instance, a group from Trpinja refused and that created some problems. The deputy of Ljubisa Petkovic went there. Was it Zoran Rankic or somebody else? Anyway, he submitted a report about lack of discipline, et cetera. However, we collected them all, disciplined them, and from then on, we integrated them into JNA units. It required some diplomatic effort, some persuasion, and most importantly I personally persuaded them that it was not any more the Communist army. It was the only army we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were people who had not served their regular military service accepted as volunteers?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: No. We admitted only persons over 18 who had done their military service, who had no convictions, and were not drinking or doing drugs. The only exception to the military service rule were women. We admitted them as nurses, but there were also very good women fighters, very capable ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were your volunteers ever sent to a training centre at Tara?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: That could have been only in 1992 or 1993. Certainly not earlier. At the time of the fighting for the Republic of Serbian Krajina, I don't believe that centre even existed. I believe Laki went there with one group, but when he saw that the Serbian police was trying to integrate our volunteers into their active-duty complement, they gave up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you able to see for what reasons did those high-ranking JNA officers want your volunteers?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: They had no choice. The mobilisation drive was unsuccessful. In Montenegro, the response was 100 per cent but in Serbia, much less. Why? Slobodan Milosevic, in fact, his regime, tried to prevent this mobilisation, tried to stand in the way because there was still the danger of the Communist generals staging a putch, sweeping out both Milosevic and Tudjman and establishing their own government with the support of the west in order to preserve the integrity of Yugoslavia. That was in their minds. This is best shown by the book of Branko Mamula, which was recently republished. Mamula supplemented it just before his death, and I read some excerpts in the newspapers. And he admits to this intention of toppling both Milosevic and Tudjman at the same time. Milosevic was aware of this and he didn't allow them to carry out the necessary mobilisation. However, on the other hand, Milosevic was supporting the sending of volunteers, of course, after our agreement with the JNA, not earlier. Before that, his police persecuted us. He knew that the JNA could never use our volunteers for their efforts to overthrow the government, to stage a putch, especially since Branko Mamula was leading this movement for Yugoslavia and that included Kadijevic, Blagoje Adzic, Aleksandar Kadijevic, Petar Simic, and so many of them. The top echelons of the army, after the League of Communists was no longer, so steeped in their own idealogy, formed their own party of generals and forced all the officers and NCOs of the JNA to become members. It was called the League of Communists - Movement for Yugoslavia. And when we reached that agreement with the JNA, my animosity towards the generals did not stop. We were sending volunteers to defend the Serbian people. However, at the same time, in the federal parliament, I was speaking openly and very vociferously against Veljko Kadijevic and the other JNA generals. I even asked for his execution in one of my speeches. If necessary, you have all these speeches in the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you were talking about this party of generals, the League of Communists - Movement for Yugoslavia, you mentioned certain names and I believe one of them is missing. So I will repeat them.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: Aleksandar Vasiljevic is missing from the transcript, if I can see well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that agreement was reached with the JNA about the participation of your volunteers, the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party within the JNA. Was this agreement really implemented?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: It was strictly implemented. And regardless of how much the army generals hated us, the top leaders of this party of generals, they still observed our agreement to the letter. Our volunteers received immediately the latest, the most modern uniforms. They were trained in the Belgrade barracks called Bubanj Potok and sometimes in other barracks too. There, they were supplied with weapons and uniformed and armed. They left Belgrade to go to the front line. They received soldiers' wages. They were not much but they received them. Their military service was written into their military service books. When a volunteer would get killed, the army would pay some small pension to the family. The army paid for the funerals. At the funeral, the army would appoint a guard of honour and army officers with bayonets on their rifles would accompany the caskets. The army sent a unit for the fire from cannons in honour of the fallen fighter. And the army also paid medical costs at the Military Medical Academy in Belgrade. So the army observed this agreement. Milosevic was also compliant. Milosevic's regime supported the sending of volunteers. Even some professional policemen from the Milosevic regime went to the front line, including Badza, for instance. Speaking of our volunteers, I can tell you for a fact about our volunteers. I wouldn't go into the issue of the other volunteers. Our volunteers got paid leave from their jobs, even a higher salary while they were on the front line. Sometimes we would supply aid to their family, winter supplies. Sometimes we provided support to the families and allowances. So when it comes to the sending of volunteers, we had the support of both of army leadership and the Milosevic regime.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just one more thing. The volunteers who were sent to the units of the Yugoslav People's Army, to whom were they answerable in case they committed a crime?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: They had to be held responsible before military courts. In the state of immediate state -- immediate danger of war, the military courts were the only competent. And even in peacetime, the military courts were the only competent to judge professional military men or men who were doing their regular military service. These military courts were abolished only sometime after 2000. However, we never received any report from the JNA. There is no such document saying that any of our volunteers had ever committed a crime anywhere. Army officers had only praise for them as courageous, disciplined and very capable. At every step, I heard only such praise. In 20 years, not even the OTP did not -- managed to find a single volunteer, to identify a single volunteer sent by me to the front line, who had committed any criminal act, any offence. It just didn't exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And one more thing. Under what insignia did your volunteers fight? Because the Yugoslav People's Army wore the five-pointed star for a while.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: At some point - I can't remember exactly when - the JNA renounced the five-point star and introduced insignia with the Yugoslav flag. However, after our agreement with the JNA, we also agreed that they would not insist on the five-pointed star. We said our volunteers would rather die than put the red Communist five-pointed star on their caps. And the army agreed. The JNA agreed that our volunteers would put the Chetnik kokarde on their caps. When they got the star insignia, they would scrape it off and put our coat of arms instead. And, by the same token, our volunteers stopped accusing and attacking the officers with a five-pointed star as Commies, traitors, et cetera. So we left all our disagreements aside and joined efforts to defend Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think it is the appropriate time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. Mr. Seselj, the Court will take its first 30-minutes' break. We'll be back at 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the break, Mr. Seselj, we talked about the replacement of the five-pointed stars with tricolour on the uniforms of the Yugoslav People's Army. I will now show you a document or, rather, a newspaper article from the time. 1D579 is the document.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: I still don't have it on my screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It will appear now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, as you know, it is helpful if you could mention the tab number of the documents you are calling.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, tab number is 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we could perhaps zoom in on the original text.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This article talks precisely about the new insignia that would replace the five-pointed red star. It is clearly stated in the last sentence. One can see that it's a decision that was adopted by the SFRY Presidency on the 16th of October. As we haven't mentioned this body so far, can you tell us what was the relation between the Presidency of the SFRY and the JNA?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: The Presidency of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia was the Supreme Command of the Yugoslav People's Army. It made such decisions as this independently after an imminent threat of war had been declared. Without such a state of emergency being declared, then the insignia of the army would have been changed by a federal law. But under the conditions of an imminent threat of war, the Presidency was authorised to issue such decrees that had the power of law.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would tender this document, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D186, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, you have said that volunteers which the Serbian Radical Party sent to the front lines to the ranks of the Yugoslav People's Army were present there. I would like us to be precise and say under whose command were they?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, they were under the command of the commanders of the units in whose ranks they fought. For example, in Vukovar, in the Operative Group South, they were part of the Motorised Guards Brigade, and in Operations Group North, they were a part of the Novi Sad Corps, so depending on where they were sent and the conditions there. In Western Slavonia, for example, they were under the command of the active-duty Colonel Trbojevic, who was the commander of Territorial Defence of Western Slavonia, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, just one moment. Mr. Seselj, could I ask you once again to observe a pause between Mr. Zivanovic's question and your answer. It could be helpful to count until ten before you start answering. That gives the interpreters the opportunity to finish their interpretation. If not, parts of your answer will be lost. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really try sincerely to make the pauses and to speak as slow as possible, but sometimes I forget it and I start speaking immediately. I guess it's a sign of old age.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that volunteers who were dispatched by the Serbian Radical Party were under the command of active-duty officers of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes. As of the 1st of September and onward, they were only under the command of the active-duty JNA officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did it last throughout the time that they spent at the fronts or the time that was recorded in their military booklets?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember if any of the high-ranking military officers said that the Serbian Radical Party volunteers were under his command?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: I received an official document from the OTP showing that the commander of the 1st Military District, General Zivota Panic, stated that Serbian Radical Party volunteers were in the JNA units; that is to say, under their command. I received that document, though I don't have it on me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We'll look at it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's P2715, tab 2. In the English translation, it's page 25, and in the original, page 26, moving onto page 27. If we could show the bottom of the page and zoom in on the original, because I think that's the section that we need.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you see the part where it says --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: I don't know what document this is. I suppose it's Panic's statement. I can see in English that it says "Panic." But one can see a bit of it in Serbian, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could move the original text to the right a little bit, please, then you will see the abbreviation.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes. That's probably the Prosecution's interview with General Zivota Panic. That's what I suppose, I suppose from the form of the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It's actually an interview given to the foreign media but, nevertheless, we shall focus on the contents of the words. At the very bottom of the page in Serbian, where it reads that: "The volunteers were Arkan's Tigers and Seselj's Chetniks. Those weren't big groups." And then it reads, if we could please move onto the next page in the original. "However, I placed all these formations under my command and they carried out the tasks of the units in which they were." Are these words of General Zivota Panic correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: Quite correct. And I would also note that we had volunteers in formations numbering 100 to 120 men, more or less the size of a company. The volunteers were headed or led by one of them who had become prominent in fighting earlier, showed himself as capable, and so on. We didn't have bigger formations because for them it was necessary to have educated officers. So our most prominent volunteers were capable of commanding units up to the size of a company.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us whether the Serbian Radical Party volunteers participated in the Vukovar operation in 1991?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, they took a very active part in it, and much credit is to be given to them that Vukovar was liberated. They participated in the activities of Operations Group South and Operations Group North.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us about Serbian Radical Party volunteers who participated in the Operations Group South? What was the unit they were deployed in?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: By command of the commander of the Motorised Guards Brigade, then Colonel and later General Mile Mrksic, all Serbian Radical Party volunteers were included in the Territorial Defence detachment Leva Supoderica, which then became part of the composition of the Guards Brigade. These were not only our volunteers; volunteers from other parties, those who appeared of their own initiative and enlisted as volunteers, and so on. Most of the members of the unit had been sent by the Serbian Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who was the commander of that unit, Leva Supoderica?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: The commander was a reserve captain Milan Lancuzanin, called Kameni.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was he a member of the Serbian Radical Party at the time?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: Not at that time. Milan Lancuzanin, called Kameni, was not a member of the Serbian Radical Party but he joined it later. First, he became our sympathiser when he saw what our volunteers were like when they were in action, and then he joined the party. I think it was in the early months of 1992. And he remains a member to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: During the Vukovar operation, did you come to the Vukovar area; and, if so --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes. I did from both sides. Twice from the south; once in October and the last time on the 8th of November. But I also showed up in Trpinja and in Borovo Selo which is to the north of Vukovar. I went to tour Tenja where there were some forward positions with our volunteers who were engaged in the fighting, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: To start from your first visit to Vukovar, could you tell us, how long did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, the first time I came in the morning and I left late in the evening. I toured all the forward front lines, and in the evening, the commander of the Guards Brigade, Colonel Mrksic, organised a dinner for me at his staff in Negoslavci. And I remember well that we ate beans with sausages and I remember also the helmet that I wore on my head was too small, and then there were some jokes about it. And the Chief of Staff of the Guards Brigade, then-Lieutenant-Colonel and now General Panic, presented me with his helmet which fitted me well. Why am I telling you all this? To let you know that these things remain etched deep in my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you meet anyone else on that occasion, for example, any political figures or civilian authorities, on the occasion of your first visit to Vukovar when you visited the Guards Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: I don't remember a single political figure that I may have met. I was only in company with military personnel - officers, soldiers, volunteers, the territorials. Just major Borivoje Trajkovic accompanied me to tour the forward front lines. There's a photograph of us walking along a wide Vukovar street that was later on published in many newspapers. Major Trajkovic, who remained a general and a commander of the gendarmerie in Serbia, complained later on that this photograph where he accompanied me embittered his life quite a lot. Once we, the radicals, started our violent fight against the Milosevic regime, then that was a hindrance in his otherwise very successful military career.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. It's just to correct something on the transcript. I believe it is page 36, line 9-10, I think the answer has gotten merged with the question. So it's just to alert that the answer needs to be separated from the question at that line. I think the answer begins at: "By command of the commander of the Motorised Brigade ..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. There's also a written order issued by Colonel Mrksic pursuant to which the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party were to be incorporated into the Leva Supoderica detachment. The OTP, I'm sure, has that order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, would you agree with Ms. Biersay's suggestion?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I agree with Prosecution that here both question and answer were joined and should be separated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Do you also agree with her suggested solution?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Noted. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please describe your second arrival in Vukovar during Operation Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: The second time I arrived in Vukovar, it was perhaps on the 8th of November. I wouldn't remember the date if I hadn't found it in the documents of the OTP. I spent two days there. I spent the night there. I toured all the forward lines. I talked to the volunteers there and their commander Lancuzanin as well as some officers that I met on the front line. On that occasion, I didn't go to Negoslavci to meet with Mrksic. I didn't want him to think that I got used to him wining and dining me. And I remember well that I spent the night in Mile Lancuzanin's, Kameni's, house. And during the night an aeroplane of the Croatian agricultural aviation in a very close vicinity towards the house threw explosives. The explosion was very powerful. It woke me up and I shared a room with Michel Binic, who was the then-president of Serbian National Association from Pristina. We were both awoken and he could not sleep after that. I just turned around and went back to sleep. In the morning, I left the house sometime around 6.00 or 7.00. One of the volunteers -- I had stripped down to the waist, and one of the volunteers poured water on me to wash my face. The reputable Serbian photographer Tomislav Peternek came by. He took my photo and later published it in the Nin magazine, and that was later on reproduced in a number of other publications.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Once the operation for the liberation of Vukovar ended, after the 18th of November, 1991, did you attend a celebration under a tent in Vukovar? Together with you there were also officers of the Guards Brigade there. For example, General Adzic was there, Petar Gracanin, Mihajl Kertes, Franko Simatovic, Goran Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: It is a pure fabrication. When Vukovar was liberated, I was in Knin. The OTP even has a video-clip dating back to that time, my conflict with Captain Dragan on the front line near Benkovac and my subsequent conversation with the volunteers. I was 400 or 500 kilometres away from Vukovar at that time. However, I visited Vukovar on the first anniversary of the liberation, or rather, on the second anniversary. I went there together with my wife Jadranka. There were several officers there at the time, but none of the people that you have mentioned in your question. Zivota Panic wasn't there. I didn't even know him then. Veljko Kadijevic or Adzic were not there. Kertes was also not there. Franko Simatovic, Frenki, wasn't there. I was the -- I met Franko Simatovic, Frenki, for the first time here in the Detention Unit of the Hague Tribunal. I had never seen him before. I never knew for a fact what he looked like, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In 1991, did you ever meet Goran Hadzic in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: No, I did not. Perhaps he was around but I don't remember a single meeting that might have taken place in 1991 and that would have involved him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Although you have already answered that question, I suppose that I should have asked you what contacts you had in the course of 1991, but you have already answered that.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: Absolutely none whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us whether and when the Serbian Radical Party was established in the Republic of Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: A few months after the war. I can't tell you exactly when, but it was duly registered in the Republic of Serbian Krajina, so the information can be easily checked. The first president was Rade Leskovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "a few months after the war," what do you have in mind? What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: After the liberation of Vukovar, after the Vance-Owen Plan was passed, after the implementation of the Vance-Owen Plan. To all intents and purposes, the war was over by then and then Croatians launched several armed aggressions with the help of Americans, and they occupied the territory of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. However, we, Serbs as a people, on the whole will never give up on the liberation of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. Some day, our sons, our grandsons, will certainly liberate the Republic of Serbian Krajina and all the other Serb territories.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us something about the relationship between the SDS in the Republic of Serbian Krajina and the Serbian Radical Party? Did they share power? Who was in power? Who was the opposition at that time?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: In 1991, there was no inter-party relationship. There were very few contacts. However, in 1993 --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I may have not been precise in my question. I am talking about the relationship between the Serbian Radical Party in the Republic of Serbian Krajina on the one hand and the SDS in the Republic of Serbian Krajina, and I'm referring to the year 1992.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: In 1992, the Serbian Democratic Party, as far as I can remember, was all ready split. One wing had separated from the rest of the party. The Serbian Democratic Party in the Federal Republic of Croatia had been set up by Jovan Raskovic and that was in 1990. However, that party was later divided. One wing seceded from the party and set up the Serbian Democratic Party of Krajina, with its seat in Knin, and it was headed by Ljubica Solaja. Subsequently, she joined the Serbian Radical Party. I don't know how things transpired in the east. I wouldn't be able to tell you. However, I believe that only after the Vance Plan -- the Vance-Owen Plan was adopted, the Serbian Democratic Party spread onto the entire territory. Before that, the eastern world remained loyal to Jovan Raskovic, but I'm not even sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, what comes to mind first when we're talking about Goran Hadzic? How do you remember him?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: In May 1993, at the initiative of the regime that was in power in Serbia, a General Serbian Assembly was called to take place in the large hall of the Sava centre in Belgrade. It was not the largest of the halls; it was the second largest. And all the MPs were invited from the Federal Assembly, the Republican Assembly of Serbia, the Assembly of Montenegro, the Assembly of Republika Srpska, and the Assembly of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. Since Slobodan Milosevic could not convince the leadership of the Republika Srpska to adopt the Vance-Owen Plan for the division of Bosnia and Herzegovina, he called the joint assembly to invite people to vote. He was hoping that a majority would be voted over. The pro-west and opposition parties in Serbia boycotted that meeting, and the People's Assembly of Republika Srpska and the Federal Assembly of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, without the MPs of the Serbian Radical Party, could not achieve a quorum. In the keynote address, the proposal was put forth to adopt the Vance-Owen Plan as the best, if not the only, solution, and so on and so forth. One of the first speakers was Goran Hadzic who was adamant. He wanted everybody to adopt the Vance-Owen Plan. He was already then the president of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. Since I thought it was already too early to embark on this size of showdown with Milosevic, I took the floor and I used all sorts of arguments to attack Goran Hadzic, and then the Serbian Radical MPs stood up and walked out of the meeting. After our departure, the General Serbian Assembly could no longer decide on anything. In other words, I used Goran Hadzic's words as a good opportunity to speak and to use that as an excuse for walking out. It was too early for me to attack Milosevic, but our relationship by then was already very tense.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, Milosevic was in favour of that option. He wanted to adopt the Vance-Owen Plan.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes. Milosevic was in favour. The president of Montenegro, Momir Bulatovic, and the entire leadership of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, headed by Dobrica Cosic, they were all in favour. Goran Hadzic as well. There was no voting. I don't know how the MPs of the Republic of Serbian Krajina would have voted. We thwarted that. However, Goran Hadzic was very much in favour. We, the Serbian Radicals, and the leadership of Republika Srpska prevented that vote, prevented that from happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just one more thing I wanted to ask you about that. After that, what was your relationship with Goran Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: There was no relationship at all. The relationship was bad, if anything. I often attacked him; he sometimes attacked me. On the eve of the elections in 1993, when we embarked on a fierce showdown with Slobodan Milosevic and the Socialist Party, he signed a proclamation saying that we were criminals. I don't know what else was there. However, we did not use words. There was no love lost between us -- between us. We lay charges against him. So our relationship was very hostile until the moment the two of us met here in The Hague. And here in The Hague, you know, as much as I fought against Milosevic here, we struck a very sincere friendship. However much I fought against Goran Hadzic, our relationship here is normal. And the same applies to some other people with whom I had conflicted before. We are all here in the same boat, as people would say, and our joint enemy is the Hague Tribunal. There's no two ways around it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When was the first time that you heard of the crime that was committed in Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: Much later than the crime itself happened. Perhaps a year later, or maybe a few months later, or perhaps even more than a year. I really couldn't be -- I couldn't tell you for a fact. However, as soon as I heard of the crime, I called Milan Lancuzanin, Kameni. He was not very talkative. To be honest, he didn't tell me much. He swore to me that he had not participated in that and that none of the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party had. After the exhumation which took place in 1993, I believe, a lot was written about that in the Serbian press, and the version that was pushed by the Serbian press was that the Guards Brigade handed over the prisoners to the civilian authorities and that the territorials then executed those prisoners. Subsequently, I learned that the situation was entirely different, and that was only when I found myself here at the Hague Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
