utterances.text: You say that inter alia in the Milosevic case you testified or, rather, one part of your testimony was about the crime committed in Ovcara. Do you remember what you said at that time?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: I remember things more or less well. But, at that time, I really believed that the prisoners had been handed over to the civilian authorities. That was my state of mind at the time. At the time I didn't have privileged contacts with my legal advisors and the team that assisted me in my defence. Later, my investigators in the field arrived at the truth, and that truth was corroborated by the documentation that the OTP has at its disposal. I knew then that during the relevant time, General Aleksandar Vasiljevic was also in Vukovar. However, the point of my accusations was the theft of several million German marks from the Vukovar bank and not the execution at Ovcara, although I had my doubts about that as well. I believe that I said that and you will probably found it in the record. I think that this is more or less what I said, but I can't say -- remember things word for word because it was nine years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I can jog your memory by reading from the paragraph in question. It's tab 19, 120805, and the page number is 61 and also 62. I'm going to read the original transcript to you and you will receive interpretation --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I don't quite understand where counsel is going with this. I believe he asked Mr. Seselj what his recollection was about testimony, so I'm not sure of the purpose of now showing him this document. I ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to remind the witness what he said during his testimony in Milosevic, and I think that it is quite legitimate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have lost the interpretation completely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I see --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The words of Ms. Biersay have not been interpreted. I'm sure that she said something really smart because that's what she always does. But I don't know what and I suppose I should know what she said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Of course, Mr. Seselj, you should get interpretation of everything that is said in the courtroom. Do you get interpretation of what I'm saying? Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, now I can hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Ms. Biersay, would you please repeat your objection or your -- no, your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: My question was there's no indication that Mr. Seselj did not remember, in essence, what he testified about. What he said he didn't remember word for word, and there's no requirement that he remember word for word and there's no need to show him these transcript pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I recall, Mr. Seselj said that he doesn't know exactly what was said but just some -- some -- some main features of his evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I do think he said "word for word." Please try to explore Mr. Seselj's memory without the text, to start with, and we'll see what happens.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, do you remember whether, on that occasion when you testified, you mentioned that your inquiries into the Ovcara case were underway?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: I said that my knowledge is conditional because my investigators were still working on the ground. I believe that's what I said then. But I would really like you to read out that passage. I cannot interpret differently all the things that I said on that occasion. I don't know who would be able to.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'm glad that Mr. Zivanovic and Mr. Seselj are so in sync, but I still have the same objection to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what objection is. I understood that the objection was accepted by the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Not really, Mr. Zivanovic. We asked you to explore whether Mr. Seselj does remember what his testimony was in the other case. Now you asked him, and his answer, in sync, as Ms. Biersay says, is "I have difficulty in remembering." So the ball is in your camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In that case, I would remind Mr. Seselj and read one passage of -- a relevant passage of his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: To which Ms. Biersay objects. One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The objection is sustained, Mr. Zivanovic. We are of the view that it is not of importance what Mr. Seselj's memory is on what he said in the other case. The important thing is what he remembers from the facts you want to question him about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you also remember that two and a half years ago in your own trial you made closing remarks.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: It was not really a closing argument. They did not allow me to make my opening statement in defence otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, for the most part, what you said in those final arguments regarding the events at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: In that case, at the very beginning, I made the statement of the accused, and at the end I had ten hours to make my closing remarks, my final arguments. My final arguments, my closing arguments, are very different from the statement I made at the beginning, the statement of the accused, because in the meantime, with the help of my investigators on the ground, I had gained a lot of new knowledge. And what I said in the closing remarks reflects that definitive knowledge, and that is based on all that I found out in the meantime and all the evidence in the case file.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember what you said in your closing argument about the execution of the prisoners at Ovcara? What knowledge did you have about that event?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: I established all this very precisely through my own work, the work of my investigators, and by reviewing a huge amount of documents. The execution at Ovcara was organised by General Aleksandar Vasiljevic, chief of the security service of the JNA, and the entire execution was carried out by officers of the security service with the participation of some members of the Guards Brigade and members of the Territorial Defence as direct executioners. I have acquired information that General Aleksandar Vasiljevic had pulled out three colonels from retirement. They were no longer active-duty officers. They were in the reserve. He reactivated them - Bogdan Vujic, Bogoljub Kijanovic, and Slavko Tomic - whom he sent to Ovcara to do the execution. Nowhere in the documentation is it said that they were reactivated. Nothing was marked in their military service booklets concerning those days. They had received no remuneration, et cetera, et cetera. They arrived at Vukovar at the same time as Vasiljevic, which means on the 19th of November, the evening of 19 November. They were accommodated at the command of the Motorised Brigade in Negoslavci. And from the 18th until the evening of the 19th, for two full days, none of the soldiers or the officers of the JNA entered the Vukovar Hospital. There were some patients in the Vukovar Hospital. There were wounded men. But there was also a large number of Croatian soldiers who had put on patients' pajamas to avoid capture. That in itself was strange. If Vukovar had fallen, the Vukovar Hospital should be taken over immediately by military regulation. Two days later, when Vasiljevic came with his assistant, Colonel Tumanov, who later became a general, Dr. Vesna Bosanac was brought from the Vukovar Hospital and a special emissary of the Croatian government, Marin Vidic, known as Bili. Vesna Bosanac, together with JNA officers Bogoljub Kijanovic, Slavko Tomic, and Bogdan Vujic, made a list of people from the Vukovar Hospital who were to be executed. Exactly 200 were executed because it had been arranged with General Vasiljevic and the Croatian government to execute 200. I don't know what interests lay behind that. I'm just stating the facts. The next morning, the JNA entered the hospital, led by Veselin Sljivancanin. All the prisoners from Vukovar, from Mitnica and other places, were transported by buses to Sremska Mitrovica. In Sremska Mitrovica, there is a large civilian prison and one section of that prison was turned into a camp for POWs. All of them were moved there, apart from 207 of them who were first brought by Sljivancanin to the Vukovar barracks, and from there he transported them to Ovcara. I cannot claim that Sljivancanin, too, participated in the execution, but he is the one who brought them there. And he didn't turn them over. He didn't hand them over to anyone. There are no documents showing that they were handed over to civilian authorities or anyone else. He just brought them there and left them to the other officers who were there on the spot. When all this had been arranged in that way, then the JNA organised the digging of the grave. A military excavator was used to do that. In fact, it was an excavator from some company in Vukovar that the army had commandeered. One officer personally oversaw the digging of the grave while it was still daylight, that is to say, the afternoon of the 20th. The execution by firing squad began that night. Statements turned up that prisoners were brought there by tractor-trailers, but according to my information, trucks were used. I don't know which vehicle it was exactly, but it was covered by tarpaulin. Tractor-trailers usually don't have tarpaulin. And they were brought in groups. Before the beginning of the execution, lists were compared. It was established that 207 prisoners were there. Seven were separated and released. Among those released were Emil Cakalic, Dragutin Berghoffer, and five more whose names I don't remember but the Prosecution knows well who I am talking about. They were released for the sole reason that they were above the figure of 200 because 200 was arranged. Why would anybody execute 202 or 207 when the arrangement was only for 200? And the whole time while they were taken for execution, the security officers were on the spot, the security officers that had been brought by Aleksandar Vasiljevic. Only towards the end of the execution those officers returned to Belgrade. Now, look at one thing. 200 people were executed and the next day, silence. Everybody keeps quiet. I cannot accuse Sljivancanin of having participated in the execution, but what did he do the next day as the responsible officer of the Motorised Guards Brigade and the security officer of the Operations Group South to find out what had happened to those 200 prisoners that he had taken to Ovcara? Everybody keeps silent. Two days later, the Guards Brigade goes back to Belgrade. Colonel Vojnovic is appointed commander of defence of Vukovar. He was the commander of the 19th Motorised Brigade. And during the execution at Ovcara, this Colonel Vojnovic was the local commander for a place that encompassed three villages in Ovcara. What did he, as the commander of Vukovar, do to inquire about the fate of those prisoners? What did the military security service do? What did General Vasiljevic do? All they did was to cover up the crime. After the liberation of Vukovar, a large special team arrived consisting of pathologists and forensics from the Military Medical Academy in Belgrade. Colonel Stankovic was one of them. He later became a general. He was even Yugoslavia's minister of defence for a while. This group of officers, medics, mainly pathologists, autopsied all the corpses. Exhumations were done wherever bodies were found. There were people who died of natural causes. There were people who died of shelling; people who died in combat. You know, when there is an armed conflict going on, nobody has time to take corpses to the cemetery. They are buried in the first place possible. They exhumed all these bodies, and after post-mortems - there is an autopsy report for each body and documentation - they were properly buried at the Vukovar cemetery. Only Ovcara wasn't touched. The exhumations at Ovcara happened only in 1993. A Croatian pathologist, Davor Strinovic, who testified in my case, confirmed when I asked him directly that exactly 200 bodies were exhumed, in fact skeletons. Exactly 200. The Croats managed to identify 193. Those were, in fact, Croatian prisoners. Seven remain unidentified to this day. Why? Because obviously they were foreigners and nobody looked for them. I suppose they were all Kurds because many Kurds were recruited into Croatian paramilitary formations for money. Now, as to how they were paid exactly is another long story. If you want me, I can tell you. But I believe we should focus on the facts relating to the execution itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Just one moment, Mr. Zivanovic. I would like to Mr. Seselj repeat for the record slowly the names of the three retired colonels he was talking about in the beginning of his answer. You see what I'm aiming at, Mr. Seselj? Three names.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those are Colonel Bogdan Vujic, Colonel Bogoljub Kijanovic, and Colonel Slavko Tomic. Slavko Tomic was so old that he had even served as an officer in the partisans. When he became the commander of the Guards Brigade, when he came to the Guards Brigade, he said that he already had good experience in how to deal with the Croats, and there were even some witnesses here who confirmed it. My investigators --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Seselj. I just wanted to have the names on the record. Please proceed, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I will ask you just to clarify two things from your answer. I think that one is on page 50 of today's transcript where you said that the execution was arranged by General Vasiljevic and the Croatian authorities. Could you tell us, where did you get that information from?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: From the work of my investigators. My investigators contacted many security officers, military security officers who were retired, many other people who were also connected with it. I discussed that with General Mrksic here on several occasions because he was prosecuted here for Ovcara. He was intimidated in Belgrade and told that he mustn't say a word or else they would liquidate his entire family. That is what General Mrksic told me. What was the reason? I believe that General Vasiljevic was blackmailed. All the indicia seems to indicate that, and the evidence. As soon as Tudjman came into power, he had his operations groups, Opera and Labrada, and he organised that a bomb be planted on the building of the Jewish municipality in Zagreb. And he also organised the mining of the Jewish cemetery at Mirogoj, in Zagreb, so that the international public would ascribe that to Tudjman's regime. However, Tudjman's state security or secret police managed to find both the Labrada and Opera groups, and many security officers who were involved were then arrested, many Croats among them. Tudjman kept them in prison. With their help, he blackmailed Vasiljevic. Vasiljevic personally flew with a group of Croatian prisoners to the Zagreb airport to exchange them for his officers who had been arrested. This is reliable information that I also got through the work of my investigators. In a contact with the Croats, it was around that 200 Croatian prisoners would be executed by firing squad so that Croatia would have powerful argument in front of the European Union against SFRY, the Croats being the victims of the war, especially as previously the Croatian paramilitary had killed many Serbian civilians near Gospic, around 150 Serbs. That was the information at the time. The role of Vesna Bosanac was to select who would be executed. And who was executed? Only those people who were not valuable in any way for Tudjman's regime. So that was the riff-raff of Vukovar, petty criminals, the Lumpenproletarijat, the poor people, and those who were well-known opponents of Tudjman's Croatian Democratic Union. These people were executed because that was the easiest way for the Croats to get rid of them, to sacrifice them, and that was the role that Vesna Bosanac played. I was willing to question Vesna Bosanac about this, and Colonel Vojnovic as well; however, they were 92 bis or ter witnesses in my own case and they did not testify in the courtroom. But the statement which was compiled by OTP on their behalf was included in the record as their statement. And as a matter of principle, I did not want to question witnesses where there was no examination-in-chief in the courtroom because such procedure is opposite to all elementary norms of the criminal law and criminal procedure. This is why I didn't pluck their feathers out, but the evidence is so striking that one cannot escape from them. Vasiljevic did this dirty job. He went back to Belgrade, and he was soon replaced from his position and retired by the Presidency of SFRY. Various arguments were used. One of them was that money was looted from the Vukovar Hospital. I suppose that the execution was also in the background. The new head of military security was the then-Colonel, later-General Nedjo Boskovic. He ordered the arrest of Vasiljevic and his prosecution, but Vasiljevic's influence on the regime structures was so huge that the process fell through and Nedjo Boskovic was also soon replaced. He then fled from Serbia to Montenegro. To this day, Aleksandar Vasiljevic has a powerful influence on the military security structures in Serbia. Many times I pointed my finger at the regime because of Ovcara. A trial was held in Belgrade, several trials as a matter of fact, where the executioners were prosecuted but also some completely innocent people. Some of those innocent people were convicted, like Dragan Milivojevic, Kimez, for example. Some were acquitted. Three members of the Serbian Radical Party also stood trial but they were all acquitted - Marko Ljuboja, Slobodan Katic, one Ceca, and so on. They were acquitted. Vojislav Kostunica's regime organised the trial in order to protect Aleksandra Vasiljevic and the military security service. When my team, which helped with the defence, requested the State Security Service of Serbia and the military security service to submit to it all documents mentioning my name, the state security service submitted some documents. Whether it was everything, I don't know. Maybe they hid something, concealed something, destroyed something. But there were so many documents that I published four books totalling 4.000 pages of small print, and the military security service told me that there was not a single document that mentioned my name. That was an outright lie because the OTP has a certain number of military documents including my name. Of course, they're all confidential documents produced by the military security service. What were other reasons and motives for this crime to be committed? The League of Communists - Movement for Yugoslavia had an additional motive. They were still expecting foreign intervention and support to topple both Milosevic and Tudjman to restore the Yugoslav Federation and for the army to do all this. They were hoping to receive such assistance from the west, just as the west vigilantly tried to preserve Yugoslavia up until the fall of the Berlin wall. So they were planning to topple both Tudjman and Milosevic, and they wanted to accuse both the Ustashas and the Chetniks parallelly of all war crimes. And the war crime in Ovcara was to be pinned down on the Chetniks, whether they were volunteers or the territorials from Vukovar, but it was a very perfidious idea which was partly applied during the trial in Belgrade. Nobody from the regime that was in power in Belgrade at the time was interested in the truth, and to this day General Aleksandar Vasiljevic remains protected. When I talked about what I know about General Vasiljevic during my trial, the then-minister of justice in Serbia told some MPs for the Serbian Radical Party that Seselj was completely right but it was impossible to prosecute anyone for this here, and it remains so. It's still not possible to prosecute him. Aleksandar Vasiljevic still has control of some people from the political and military ranks. Sometimes he has actual documents; sometimes there are false documents. You know that the military security service in the Communist era was considered by the dissidents as much more dangerous and much more perfidious than the civilian State Security Service. What the military security service was capable of planting on people surpasses Orwellian visions, anything that we ever read about totalitarian regimes anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As you have mentioned General Vasiljevic many times, would you tell us, since when did you know him and what were your relations with him before those events?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: I know him very poorly. I examined him and questioned him in the federal assembly when I was the president of the inquiry board that was in charge of doing the inquest of Pavle Bulatovic, who was the defence minister, and I published all the information in the book of the same title. I heard many bad things about him even before, and I began to attack him very early on. And he, for his part, returned that as perfidiously as he could. For example, through Draskovic's magazine Srpska Rec, he launched the piece of information that I had been raped in the Zenica prison and similar disgusting details. And then I realised that Vuk Draskovic had close links with Aleksandar Vasiljevic in 1990, and that Aleksandar Vasiljevic took him in his car to a meeting with General Blagoje Adzic. Vuk Draskovic published that in his book, "The Target," "Meta" in Serbian. I think that's the title of his book. So he confessed to that himself. As early as at that time, Vuk Draskovic had links with the military security service. That's where his anger at Milosevic came from because the military security service attempted to topple Milosevic up until May 1992. It was only when around 40 generals were sent into retirement, with General Blagoje Adzic first among them, could Milosevic feel some relief for the first time and begin to think that there was no danger for him from the army. Up until that time, that was -- the army was the Damocles sword hanging over his head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, it is that time. But I do want to tell you again that the witness, Mr. Seselj, is going way beyond your question, in particular, with regard to this last question of yours and the answer he gave. Way beyond his relation -- the witness's relation with the general. But, again, it's your time. Mr. Seselj, we'll go for the second break, 30 minutes, and we will be back at 12.45. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, you may proceed. I think you have 40 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I understood, it is 45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: We will not discuss five minute, Mr. Zivanovic; 45, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, could you tell us, when did you meet Radovan Stojicic, Badza?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: I met Radovan Stojicic, Badza, in 1991 in Erdut. At the time he was the commander of the Territorial Defence of SBWS under the command of Novi Sad Corps. He held a training centre in Erdut. In one period that was where we sent our volunteers after we had started co-operating with the JNA. The volunteers would stay there for a few days for basic training and were then deployed to various sections of the front. I once visited this place. I was present when a group of our volunteers arrived in several buses. I stayed there for dinner, and I stayed for the night. That was the first time in my life I met Radovan Stojicic, Badza.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know where he had worked before he became the commander of the SBWS Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: He worked in the Serbian police. I think he was a commander of some special unit. He then enlisted as a volunteer. He went to the front. He kept his status rights in the police just like everyone else. He became a prominent person there, and when he returned to Serbia, he very quickly was promoted to the deputy minister. He was a very capable man. He was courageous and later on he showed some other tendencies because of which I publicly attacked him. It's unimportant now because we are discussing 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether at the centre in Erdut Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, was also present? Did you ever have a chance to see him there as well when you visited?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, he was there with his unit then, and we met at the time. I was astonished, for example, when Badza took me and some other people to dinner. Arkan's men had already had dinner and Arkan interrupted them in the middle. He commanded them to stand up and ordered them to pray, which I found astonishing because in the former JNA it was unusual to interrupt soldiers while eating unless an alert was given. But he wanted to boast and show that his unit was religious so he arranged this, which we all found to be strange, and some of us even laughed at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt and this could wait until cross, but I didn't want to lose the transcript while we had it. He said he commanded them to stand up, and it wasn't clear from the transcript who the "he" is referring to, so I wondered if we could clear it up while we were here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I will clarify it with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you said that he ordered them to interrupt their dinner and to pray, who did you mean?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: I meant his unit. I'm not sure if it was the whole unit, but there were many of them in the hall. It was a big hall where the soldiers mess was. I'm not sure what exact facility it was, but I remember it was a big room. So he ordered his soldiers -- he couldn't order anyone else. And we were standing in line and waiting to help ourselves, you know, because it was self-service. We were carrying trays and we would help ourselves to dinner, like all other soldiers. We were not treated specially. We would never have asked that, nor would we have accepted anything that would make us different in any way from the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just to clarify because you mentioned both Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, and Radovan Stojicic, Badza. I think it remains unclear in the transcript who was the one who ordered the soldiers to stop eating and to pray? Was that Radovan Stojicic, Badza, or Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: I said that it was Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, who commanded his unit or the part of his unit that was present. I didn't count them but there were quite few of them there. Even Badza commented with us that this was improper and the like. You know, Arkan is a man with no schooling, no education at all, but he was quite intelligent and very dangerous.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I will ask you some questions about him as well a bit later. Could you now tell us this: When you were in Erdut this time, did you gain an impression and could you tell us what was the relation between Radovan Stojicic and Arkan? Was one of them subordinated to anybody else?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: Radovan Stojicic, Badza, was the main man and Arkan had to listen to him. There was also a private aspect of their relations. They could joke between themselves and so on. Badza's command position was unquestioned, but Arkan was somewhere there close to his level.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember approximately the time when you visited Erdut?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: It was in the fall of 1991. I cannot remember the exact date. It may have been recorded somewhere, but I really cannot remember. We spent the night there and on the following day I was in Borovo Selo and in Trpinja; I went to Tenja. And I had to be transported on a tractor trailer through a cornfield that had been harvested all the way to Tenja because the Croats targeted the regular road by sniper fire, and the corn had been cut in summer. But it's difficult for me to tell you the exact date, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And can you tell us, though it seems to me that it follows from your answer, if fighting was still ongoing at the time or if it had ended?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: No, no, there was still fighting going on. It must have been before my visit to Vukovar, so the fighting was in full swing. I was at the forward front line in Tenja and I even shot from a Browning machine-gun in the direction of the enemy positions. I cannot guarantee that I hit anyone but I did my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you now please tell us, since when did you know Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: I met him personally in 1990. However, I publicly attacked him as early as 1996. I wrote criminal reports to the federal prosecutor against Stane Dolanc, who was a member of the Presidency -- no, he was then the head of all secret police intelligence and counter-intelligence services as a member of the SFRY Presidency. And I accused Stane Dolanc with arguments of the murder of the emigre Stjepan Djurekovic and the head of the federal security service, Zdravko Mustac. I heard that he was recently extradited to Germany from Croatia because of the murder of Djurekovic. I had information that Arkan was one of the executors and that Stane Dolanc gave him a pistol as a gift which had an inscription, "To Zeljko from Stane." So that was in the 1980s. And I was waging a real war against Stane Dolanc at the time. In 1990, all the supporters of the football club Red Star joined the Serbian Chetnik movement, and at some point in October 1990, through mediators, Arkan requested to meet me. I said, "We can do that at the Ruski Tsar restaurant." I didn't want to go to any secret place where someone could kill me so easily. Arkan came with another man who was as tall as me but much stronger. It was -- there was one Suca who was our member but then joined Arkan's group, and he was a colonel in Arkan's Serb Volunteer Guard. Arkan was very polite at the beginning of the conversation. He told me, "I respect you as a man and as a politician. I'm not interested in politics, but I won't let anyone take over Zvezda and Delija." Those were the supporters, the fan club of the football club Red Star. "And I'm asking you to leave the Delija be." But I told him, "They have joined the Serbian Chetnik movement. They stay there. You cannot change it." And then he said, "Look, I have killed many people. You haven't killed anyone yet. So take care what you do." I quipped by saying that it was true that I hadn't killed anyone yet, "But you would be the first," I told him. On the following day, the daily press, the daily newspaper Novosti Plus, published a report covering one whole page in their report about this incident. Arkan was armed. I also had a 7.65-millimetre Browning on me. If it came to settling accounts, I wonder what it would look like. Probably I would stand no chance, but at least I showed him that he wouldn't treat me so easily. I'm not boasting, but it is realistic. I wanted to show you how much power Arkan had. I was the only man in Serbia who was capable of publicly, directly and openly opposing Arkan. No one else dared to do that, including Milosevic himself. That's how dangerous Arkan was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, just one moment to have a correct record. At the beginning of page 63, line 1, Mr. Seselj answers, "I met him," and it's Arkan, "I met him personally in 1990. However, I publicly attacked him as early as," and then it says "1996" but we heard 1986. Mr. Seselj, is that right? Did you say: "However, I publicly attacked him as early as ..."?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1986, four years before we actually met for the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now it's clear on the record. Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me, you said that in 1986 you filed a criminal report for the murder of Stjepan Djurekovic against Stane Dolanc and others. Was that criminal report also against Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: The criminal report was not against him but he was part of that content, because Arkan's participation and his attitude towards Stane Dolanc emphasised the responsibility of Stane Dolanc. Arkan was not my target but Dolanc was. Arkan was just an illustration to prove that Dolanc committed crimes. However, even then Arkan was very dangerous and the police couldn't do anything against him. He opened fire on the police. He beat them. On one occasion he was even arrested, but he was immediately released upon the order of the federal security service.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, in that criminal report, you did mention his name as somebody who participated in that murder?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: The first name, the last name, and the nickname, Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan. I published that in a book of mine which was reprinted several times, and the Prosecution has copies of those criminal reports that I filed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You've mentioned the name of a person whose nickname was Suca. I don't think that this was recorded. However, would you please repeat the context in which you mentioned him?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: His name was Nebojsa. His family name escapes me. His nickname was Suca. And he was one of the principal leaders of Red Star fans. He joined the Chetnik movement in the summer of 1990. When I conflicted with Arkan, he moved Under Arkan's reign. Let me just say that in October 1990, I was arrested and spent 23 days in jail, and then Arkan managed to snatch the Delijas from me. Perhaps in cahoots with somebody from the regime, he bribed them by giving them jobs and paying them for those jobs. That's how he managed to win almost all of them over, including Suca. This Nebojsa, Suca, later became and colonel in Arkan's volunteer guards. Arkan himself bestowed the rank upon him. And even later than that, he was killed in a showdown and that murder was never solved.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us something that was mentioned in your case and in our case. This is a formation known as the Red Berets. What do you know about that formation or those formations?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: There were many formations which the people called the Red Berets. However, that was not the official name of any of them. As far as I can remember, the first group that was known as the Red Berets were those who were trained in the training centre Golubic, near Knin, headed by Kapetan Dragan. And then during the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in Republika Srpska, there were also the Red Berets which represented the military police of the Army of Republika Srpska or its scout detachments. For example, the Bratunac Brigade had a unit of scouts which all the soldiers and the people there used to call the Red Berets because that's what they sported on their heads. In the Light Cavalry Brigade there was also a unit that wore that name, and then the OTP of the Hague Tribunal started claiming that those were the Red Berets of the Serbian MUP. They put their foot in their mouth because those were locals who sported red caps. And then sometime in 1996, a unit was officially formed in Serbia. It was a special purpose unit belonging to the Serbian state security and that unit was also popularly known as the Red Berets. So when one says "the Red Berets," it doesn't mean anything on its own. It begs a clear definition as to what unit is being referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Kapetan Dragan. Could you please tell us about the relationship between you and Kapetan Dragan?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: In 1991, I met Kapetan Dragan only once on the front line near Benkovac. I toured the Serbian positions there. He turned up out of the blue. He started talking to me and we clashed right there and then in front of the soldiers. How come I was there in mid-November? I went there to tour the volunteers and the front line in Western Slavonia. I took a JNA helicopter which was assigned to me with two officer pilots. It was the commander of the air force, General Bozidar Stefanovic, who assigned it to me. I arrived in Banja Luka, and from Banja Luka, I took a car to Western Slavonia. After I had toured all the front lines and our volunteers, I returned to Banja Luka. I had a rally there, and the hall was full of soldiers. After the rally I went to the Hotel Bosna to spend the night there, and I fully expected that on the following day the helicopter would take me back to Belgrade. And then two officials of the Serbian Democratic Party from Banja Luka came; one was Vukic and the other one's name I can't remember. They told me that they had spoken to Milan Babic and that Milan Babic was begging me to come to Knin as soon as possible because Kapetan Dragan had appeared, that he is wreaking havoc among the soldiers on the front line, and that his intention was to organise a putch. That same night I sat in a car with the two of them. I went to Knin. I was in a military uniform because in Western Slavonia I had toured our soldiers on the front line. When I arrived in Knin, I first met with Milan Babic and then I toured the army on various front lines. And I also appeared in a radio show on Radio Knin and on the youth radio. Both those shows lasted for a couple of hours. And I denounced the role of Kapetan Dragan fully. His objective was to topple Milan Babic and his government because there were many people who did not like Milan Babic. The regime in Serbian didn't, Kapetan Dragan didn't. Many didn't like Milan Babic. I successfully completed my mission and I had a final verbal skirmish with Kapetan Dragan in Benkovac. And that was recorded by a camera and, as part of their war booty, when Croatians carried out aggression against the Republic of Serbian Krajina, got hold of that clip and The Hague OTP has it. I saw it for the first time when it was shown to me in the courtroom by the OTP of this Tribunal. That was at the same time when Vukovar was liberated. It coincided with the liberation of Vukovar. I returned to Belgrade by helicopter via Mostar, and then from there on to Podgorica, and then I took a regular flight to Belgrade from there, because the small Gazelle helicopter could not fly the stretch from Knin to Belgrade. That's why I had to change helicopters. I landed at Mostar airport, and from there I flew to Podgorica in another helicopter with a different crew.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In my view -- or, rather, you mentioned Western Slavonia in your previous answer and you did so before, and you said that there were your volunteers there as well. Can you just briefly tell us what was going on in Western Slavonia? How were your volunteers involved there? How long were they deployed there?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: We had a couple hundred volunteers there. I can't remember the exact name -- number, but the most numerous volunteers from Serbia, they were on the forward front lines. That's where they were deployed. They were under the command of Colonel Trbojevic. And when I toured their lines there, I met up with Trbojevic in –- on mount Zvecevo a month later, and he had only words of praise for their discipline and valour. Western Slavonia was defended by the Territorial Defence, but that Territorial Defence was under the authority of the Banja Luka Corps of the JNA. I don't know the official name of the Banja Luka Corps, but it was the Banja Luka Corps. And since I'm in November or, rather, the beginning of December, Aleksandar Vasiljevic appeared there. Wherever he appeared, he wreaked havoc, he caused problems --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Can you look at the court reporter's note.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, I didn't notice it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, the court reporter is kindly asking you to slow down for the purposes of the record because they cannot record all your words.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: I'll do my best. I believe that from time to time I do manage to slow down, but then I go back to my own old ways. Sometime in the month of December, Aleksandar Vasiljevic came to Western Slavonia. Wherever he appeared, the units started withdrawing with no reason whatsoever. There was panic among the people and the people started withdrawing with the troops, and finally it was all pure chaos. There was no military reason for the chaos. Obviously, the Croats launched an offensive with their military and police forces, and the Banja Luka Corps didn't do anything. They were twiddling their thumbs. And volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party put up a decisive defence in Maseva Vusavela [phoen] village. In just one day, 11 volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party were killed. Some were wounded and taken prisoners. They were later exchanged after having been ill-treated in prison. The Serbs managed to consolidate their forces only in Okucani and in Pakrac. The rest of the territory fell. Vasiljevic had arrived with the intention of wreaking havoc among the Serb soldiers and in that way to hand over Western Slavonia into the Croatian hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what happened with the Serbian civilians who resided in Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: A lot of Serb civilians were killed. I don't know how many, but the number is huge. Croatians pounded from all sorts of weapons. They targeted columns of refugees with the intention of killing them on the streets, through which the civilians who were withdrawing were awash with blood.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us something about the police of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, i.e., the police which was also known as Martic's police? Do you know anything about them?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: It was the municipal police of Knin. That's who they called Martic's police. And then when the Autonomous Province of Krajina was proclaimed, then the authority of that police stretched all over Krajina. That Martic's police never encompassed all of the territories of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, until 1992 when the Republic of Serbian Krajina was proclaimed and united the western parts, Dalmatia, Lika, Kordun, there remaining western -- Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem. During combat, those police units were completely independent and divided into various forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any contacts at the time of combat, did you have any contacts with Milan Martic and those police units of his?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: When I toured their positions, I also talked to the policemen, soldiers, volunteers. I made no distinction among them. I was on good terms with both Milan Babic and Milan Martic at that time. Later on, the relationship with Martic deteriorated because together with Goran Hadzic, Martic assigned that proclamation against me and the Serbian Radical Party in the autumn of 1993. However, in 1994, at Martic's initiative, we met secretly in Beli Manastir. He apologised for having done what he did, he said he regretted that he did it, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that towards the end of 1993 in the Republic of Serbian Krajina elections for president were held?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes. If I'm not mistaken, there were four candidates: One was Milan Babic, representing the SDS of Krajina; there was Goran Hadzic on the ticket of the Party of Serbian Lands; Milan Martic and Rade Leskovac from the Serbian Radical Party of the Serbian Krajina. Milan Babic and Milan Martic went into the second round. We, the Radicals, supported Milan Babic in the second round in the runoff, but many other Serbian political parties supported Milan Martic. I believe Karadzic did, Milosevic did, groups of Belgrade intellectuals and academicians who even participated in his election campaign. Martic had a lot more support than Babic and still, in the runoff, Babic won.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And in the initial round of the elections, whom did the Serbian Radical Party support?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: We had our candidate in the first round, Rade Leskovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As a deputy to the Republic of Serbia parliament and the federal parliament, do you remember, do you know if the Federation or the Republic of Serbia provided any financial assistance to the Republic of Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: The Republic of Serbia assisted both the RSK and Republika Srpska. They helped financially. They helped in kind in every way. It's no secret. Serbia has to help Serbs wherever they are. And the federal state also helped, provided aid and funds.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was it done through the budget, through some official cash flows, or was it some kind of illegal financing?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: It went through official channels. Maybe there was some illegal financing, too. I don't know. I was not directly involved. But everybody in Serbia knew that assistance was being provided to Republika Srpska and the Republic of Serbian Krajina, and nobody objected. Not even the pro-western opposition dared to attack the regime over that. Some opposition parties even blamed Milosevic for not helping enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll ask you just one more question. Sorry, it's not going to be just one more question. There will be two. You must have heard in your own trial, and we have heard here, that many crimes --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Objection. It's leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please do, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Have you ever heard in the course of your trial --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: The same objection, Your Honour. Mr. Zivanovic should simply put a question to the witness which he will answer, but asking him whether he's heard something is leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In my understanding, it is not leading at all. I ask him to say whether he heard something or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The objection is overruled. Please continue, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Have you heard in the course of your trial that Chetniks, Seselj's Men, or the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party, had committed any crimes on the territory of the Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: The OTP tried at the beginning to label all Seselj's Men as criminals, and after the Prosecution case, they gave up. In the evidence of the Prosecution, the Chetniks were clearly separated from Seselj's Men. Yes, all the Chetniks were Seselj's Men but not vice versa. And the Prosecution referred to Serbian forces, including Seselj's Men, and Seselj's Men were not clearly identified anywhere as perpetrators of crimes. They did try to ascribe to us various individuals and groups as Seselj's Men, but they had absolutely no proof of that. Thus, the Prosecution does not have a shred evidence that any volunteer of the Serbian Radical Party sent by us from Belgrade to the front line ever committed any crime. It simply does not exist. There is, of course, the formulation of JCE --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, could you bring the witness back to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, if you could just tell us if you have any knowledge that any of the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party ever committed any crimes in the area of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, or the Republic of Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: No, not a single report. Because if that had happened, I would have been the first one to react. I could not bring them to justice but I could stigmatise them publicly, and I never shied away from stigmatising certain types of behaviour, regardless of who was responsible. There were no such things among the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party, but you have to bare in mind one more thing. There was quite a lot of turnover among the volunteers. For instance, one man would go to the front line as a volunteer of our party. He would serve one tour of duty, come back, and then he would go on his next tour of duty on behalf of another group of volunteers. For instance, sometimes Arkan and I would meet at a funeral of somebody who initially was our volunteer and later joined Arkan's Men and died as a member of the Arkan's guard. But since we knew the man and he was initially our volunteer, it was only a matter of decency for me to go attend his funeral.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to also ask you, do you know -- do you know that among the senior officers and commanders of the JNA, such as Kadijevic and Adzic, or political leaders such as Slobodan Milosevic, Milan Martic, Milan Babic, Goran Hadzic, do you know that some kind of plan or understanding was reached or any kind of arrangement to carry out ethnic cleansing of non-Serbs from Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: It did not happen. Absolutely not. I give you my own guarantee. All the instructions always said: Protect the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Seselj. I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Biersay, are you ready for cross?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: If I could have just one moment to reorganise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: Was I supposed to say something now? I'm answering your questions. This was not a question. You just noted that it was a good afternoon, at least that's the interpretation I got. You noted that this afternoon was good. Did you ask me anything? I didn't understand if it was interrogative.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: It wasn't, and you're absolutely correct. And if could you keep it in mind as we go through the cross-examination, your answers to Mr. Zivanovic were very long, and so if we could work together to make the answers just a little bit shorter to assist the interpreters, it would be helpful. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes. And I will try to be as brief as possible, but sometimes things need to be made clear and precise. Otherwise, the Trial Chamber could fail to understand, and that's something I care about.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Then we both care about it. Good. I want to go back to something that you said about Ovcara. You said, I believe it was at page 55 of the transcript - I'm not sure if this is exactly the phrasing - but what I wrote down was where you said: "Many times I pointed my finger at the regime because of Ovcara." Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: Over Ovcara? That's not what I said. In my mind, I got Ovcara completely clear here in The Hague, working on my own trial, sending my own investigators in the field, reviewing many documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: We'll get to that, Mr. Seselj. There's no question before you at this time. You, just a few minutes ago, said that you're not afraid of stigmatising people publicly. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: I didn't say exactly stigmatise. I said publicly accuse, if I believe people had done something they shouldn't have done. I didn't use the word "stigmatise"; I used the word "accuse." This term "stigmatise" has a slightly more negative connotation than the word to accuse, at least in our language.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Let me -- please, Mr. Seselj --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: When you say "accuse" --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: One moment, please. I understood your answer and now I'm going to ask you a question. My question to you is: Based on what you've told the Trial Chamber today, did you ever look at Vesna Bosanac and accuse her during your trial of preparing a list of 200 people who were to be executed at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: You did not let me do it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: My question -- we can get to that. But my question first is: Did you do it?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: How could I, if you didn't even lead her through examination-in-chief here. Instead, you automatically adopted her statement into evidence, and you knew by then that I refused to cross-examine witnesses who were not examined in-chief here in the courtroom, because I want to examine a witness based on what he himself said -- please, I haven't finished yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, one moment --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: Not based on what you wrote.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: One moment --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: You wrote her statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: One moment. Am I to understand what you're saying as, because she was a 92 ter witness, you decided not to ask her any questions?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: I did not decide not to ask her any questions. I decided not to ask any questions of anyone who appeared in the courtroom under Rule 92 ter because I continue to consider this rule as illegal. It was adopted against all legal principles. It was brazen arbitrariness by the Judges of the Hague Tribunal, and it was adopted in a later version. It did not exist in the beginning. They learned that it was very useful in the Milosevic trial. You don't seem happy with my answers but have you to hear me out till the end.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Your answers are your answers. My only issue is that I'm asking you to answer the question in a concise way, and I will follow up with additional questions. So if I understand you correctly now, what you are -- are you saying that you did ask Vesna Bosanac on the 5th and 6th of November, 2008, about whether or not she ordered 200 people to be executed at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that the witness asked and answered to this question that he didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Biersay. Mr. Seselj, Mr. Seselj, I would ask you when objections are made and we try to get to a decision on objections, I would ask you not to intervene unless we ask you to intervene. Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj has, of course, explained his objection to the 92 ter process used at this Tribunal, and I'd like to get a very clear answer from him about whether or not he ever put it to Bosanac on the 5th and 6th of November, 2008, the accusation he is publicly making regarding her involvement in executing 200 people at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, didn't you hear me? Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I understand, Mr. Seselj said that he did not -- did not cross-examine any witness whose Rule 92 ter statement was admitted into evidence, and in my understanding, Mrs. Bosanac was among these witnesses.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I say something, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe it could assist you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It's asked and answered, Ms. Biersay. Please move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: But you did make these accusations against Vesna Bosanac when you gave your closing in March 2012; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: Towards the end of Vesna Bosanac's testimony, I strenuously objected against the decision of the Trial Chamber, saying that the Trial Chamber had allowed the monster from the Vukovar Hospital to file through the courtroom unpunished, scot-free. You can find the documentation reflecting it because I cannot repeat it verbatim. And by examining certain other witnesses, I insisted on the same, for instance, witness Vukasinovic - was that the name? - Colonel Ljubisa Vukasinovic, and some others.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So my question to you is: Did you make these accusations against Vesna Bosanac when you gave your closing in March of 2012?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: If I remember well, yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Are you aware that Dr. Bosanac testified in the case against Goran Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So you don't know that she testified in April of 2013?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: If she had testified, the OTP would have been duty-bound to give me a transcript of her testimony because it concerns my trial. I have never received that transcript. If you claim I did, you should show me a receipt. And in case that I had received it, I haven't read it. But you should send me some proof because it is your obligation.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Do you know that it was never put to Dr. Bosanac the accusation that she selected 200 people to be executed at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: Why didn't you put it to her? Why did you stop me from putting it to her?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: The Defence did not put it to Dr. Bosanac in this case; did you know that?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that. But how could I be informed of what the Defence team in this case knew or didn't know? I had a couple of proofing sessions with Mr. Zivanovic, but we discussed things that I could possibly testify about. I did not question him about his earlier work or how he examined this or that witness, nor did he mention to me the witnesses who had appeared here, especially not the witnesses of the Prosecution. I don't remember a single one. He insisted that I give him the most elaborate possible account of my knowledge rather than sharing his knowledge based on his examination of earlier witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And you and Mr. Hadzic have been together at the Detention Unit since 2011; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, we have, but we see each other very rarely because we are in different blocks. We have never shared the same block. But we would meet sometimes when we both were receiving visits or when somebody would ask me from a different floor, is this Hadzic or Lukic or Tolimir. They would invite me to some sort of celebration to a different block and then I would get to meet the people who live in that block. We don't have an opportunity on a daily basis to meet each other. If both our wives are visiting, then we may find ourselves in the same section of the Detention Unit. If I go to the other floor, we can exchange a few words, but we were never together, strictly speaking.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And, as you say, you and Mr. Hadzic are in the same boat at the Detention Unit; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, if the question could be clarified, what does it mean, "same boat"?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: This is the language used by Mr. Seselj and that's exactly what I'd like to know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If memory serves me well, I never mentioned a boat. I said we were now in the same, and then I didn't pronounce the next word because, in the Serbian language, it's a four-letter word. It's a profanity. The Serbian people know what I meant, and if you insist, I can tell you, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Today you described over many transcript pages what you believed happened at Ovcara; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes. It's not what I think. It's what I maintain. It's what I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And you know this even though you were not at Ovcara; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: I was not at Ovcara. I cannot lay an egg, but while eating an egg, I can judge whether it's a good one or not. I learned about the crime subsequently. But when I found myself in The Hague, I started an intensive investigation, an inquiry, especially since only five years later, the Hague Tribunal registered my legal advisors so I could talk to them without being eavesdropped on. That was not before I --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: -- went through a hunger strike to win some rights for myself and to get rid of the assigned counsel who was imposed on me.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I understand. So when you testified in the Milosevic case, you had a different view of what the evidence showed; is that correct? About Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: No, you couldn't say that it was a different view because I then also mentioned Aleksandar Vasiljevic and other elements. But I remember well that I said then that my investigators were working on it. They were still working on it, and I'm sure you have it recorded somewhere. The information I had at the time was that the army really handed over the prisoners to the civilian authorities. All the Serbian press wrote about that. No one in the Serbian public ever mentioned a different version. I had no idea about that. While preparing for my defence after my legal advisors had been registered, I clarified these matters in my mind, and I'm telling you what I have learned about this, so the various information I received from various sources.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And who -- Mr. Seselj --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: My mindset was such at the time and now it is as it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Who was your primary source for the information that you had back when you testified in the Milosevic case?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: I didn't have any sources at the time. I was then saying off the top of my head what I knew then.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: In your --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: And what I believed to be true. I did not have any sources at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: And I learned from the Serbian press what I knew about it then.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: In the statement that you provided to the Hadzic Defence in paragraph 78, I read the English version: "During my testimony in the Slobodan Milosevic case, I had other information, primarily from JNA sources, which I believed to be true. That is why I stated that the government of the SO," meaning Serbian District "of SBZS had taken over the prisoners who were executed at Ovcara."

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: But how come that Hadzic appears in the transcript now? I never heard that you mentioned him and here's Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Let me clarify. In the statement that you provided to the Hadzic -- the Defence, the one that you signed this year, I am reading a paragraph from that statement. So what I've just read to you is what is in English, in paragraph 78 --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: -- of your statement.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: Ms. Biersay, the first name that appears here is Hadzic, where it is reads "Serbian District of SBZS." Now it's been erased after my intervention. Here on the screen, in the transcript. Not in my statement. Ms. Biersay, all the Serbian press published information that --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, one moment.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: You don't want to hear any of my answers.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I do, most definitely. But what I'm saying is you said you really had no sources, and in paragraph 78 you say it came from JNA sources, so I'm trying to reconcile those two statements.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ
utterances.text: I find it strange that you did not understand it properly, Ms. Biersay, because according to my estimate you're an intelligent woman. My information came from the JNA sources. What the JNA served the public is the only thing that was available in the Serbian public. An investigation was conducted before a military court in Belgrade. Veselin Sljivancanin and I think Mrksic and some others were examined. The result of the investigation was that they were found not guilty but that the prisoners handed over and then shot by firing squad. You should have the complete materials from the investigation. You would then see that the JNA security service fabricated the information and used it to deceive the public. Up until I came to The Hague, I had no idea about this. I met General Mrksic sometimes and I learned many things from him.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'm sure you did. I would now like to read to you a section of your testimony in the Milosevic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry for the intervention or interrupting, but the last sentence of Mr. Seselj's was not transcribed or translated. He mentioned General Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It's "after the JNA security service fabricated the information and used it to deceive the public"?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It's line 8. After the last sentence in line 8, one whole sentence was omitted from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: "... fabricated information and used to deceive the public. I came to The Hague. I had no idea about this," and then there is something missing, you're saying, Mr. Zivanovic. Mr. Seselj, is there something missing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was about to say that I had several meetings with General Mrksic here, how General Mrksic told me the details about what happened, and primarily, which I believe to be of most importance, General Mrksic told me not only about threats to his family but he also told me that for almost a month he was being prepared at military land in Dobanovci. He could go hunting there and he had other diversions, but every day for four hours, security officers worked with him. Their goal was that he wouldn't speak about anything important here. First of all, they wanted to serve him with a version that would be most favourable for them, and then they realised that it would be best if he never testified, so he did not testify in his own case.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'm not sure if that clarifies the Court's question, but it certainly was lengthy. And I note the time and I would conclude here for the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Seselj, we'll finish for the day. We'll all be back tomorrow at 9.00. You are still a witness. You remain a witness as long as you are on the stand, which means that you cannot discuss your testimony with anybody and you cannot communicate with either of the parties, Defence and OTP. Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Though I would gladly contact Ms. Biersay, if possible, as I find her really nice as a character. It's just a small joke. I hope you don't hold it against me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 10th day of September, 2014, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.00 p.m.,
